Meeting header:

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: All right everyone, thanks for joining. we wanted to run through the POC scope — specifically capacity sizing and autoscale strategies, um for the Acme Health use case. 
00:18 Maya: Thanks. Quick note, our peak is mostly during the clinician shift change window, about 9:30 to 11:00 local, which maps to that 8 to 10am UTC you mentioned. We need to make sure latency holds up, p95 under 350ms ideally.
00:35 Jordan: okay p95 350 — got it. Samira, can you start with the high-level options?
00:42 Samira: Yeah. So there are basically three levers: reserved GPUs (dedicated capacity), burst pools (short-lived extra instances), and fallbacks to cheaper model variants — e.g., int8 quantized or smaller context models. For the POC we usually propose a small reserved baseline (1-2 GPUs) plus a burst policy to add capacity when queue length spikes.
01:05 Rafael: Couple quick Qs — what does burst pricing look like vs reserved? And how do you manage cold starts for burst nodes?
01:12 Jordan: Price delta is in the worksheet I'll send — typically burst is higher unit-cost but you only pay when it's used. Cold starts: we have a warm pool and fast spin-up paths; for GPUs it can be 30s to 90s depending on model and image, though we try to mitigate via a tiny pre-warmed pool.
01:34 Priya: 30 to 90 seconds is a lot for clinical workflows — can we guarantee fallback so that if a burst is still booting we route to a quantized variant without blowing up quality?
01:45 Samira: Exactly — that's the fallback policy. We define a chain: preferred model (fp16 large), fallback to int8 equivalent, then smaller architecture if necessary. We also do prefix/KV cache to speed up session continuation. The trade is inference quality vs latency/cost.
02:05 Tom: On the infra side, how much headroom do you recommend reserving? 1 GPU per X concurrent sessions?
02:12 Evan: It depends on model and sequence length. For a 7B model at 1,024 context average, we typically estimate 80-120 RPS per A100 for streaming small responses, but for chat with longer contexts it's more like 8-20 concurrent reasonable sessions. For safety during POC we usually size to observed peak QPS and add 20-30% buffer.
02:38 Maya: We can give you a 7-day traffic trace. It includes average tokens per request and session lengths. We'll upload to the shared drive.
02:46 Jordan: Perfect. Rafael, can you share by Monday?
02:50 Rafael: Yeah trying for Monday, will anonymize.
02:54 Samira: For benchmarks we'll run two passes: steady-state throughput (to validate reserved capacity) and spike tests (to validate burst scaling and fallback correctness). Spike tests include sudden 10x bursts for 1-5 minutes.
03:15 Priya: For success criteria, besides p95 latency, we want to track correctness metrics — hallucination rate on a labeled prompt set and token cost per session.
03:27 Jordan: Noted. We'll include example eval harness. We'll also track SLOs: 99.9% availability during the clinician window and p95 latency target.
03:37 Maya: Timeline — what are you expecting for the POC length and milestones?
03:42 Samira: Typical POC: 6 weeks. Week 0-1: sizing + infra prep. Week 2: baseline benchmarks on reserved cluster. Week 3-4: burst and fallback tests + quality evals. Week 5-6: stabilization, runbook, and handoff. We can compress if both sides prioritize.
04:02 Rafael: If we want a faster path, could we start with a hosted small POC first then move to dedicated?
04:07 Jordan: Absolutely — hosted is fastest to iterate. But since you have compliance concerns (PHI-ish), we discussed Private / VPC earlier — we can do a private POC but it takes longer to provision. There's a middle ground: dedicated isolated pool in our cloud region with audit logging.
04:23 Tom: On security: will logs contain raw prompts? We need KMS support and audit log retention policy.
04:29 Jordan: Yes, options: redact / token-level policy, and we support customer-managed KMS for Private/Dedicated. We'll include SOC2 & data flow docs.
04:40 Priya: Back to scaling numbers — Evan, can you walk through an example calc for our traces?
04:46 Evan: Sure: say you have 1,200 peak concurrent sessions in that 90-minute window, average response length 180 tokens, avg model latency per token ~12ms on A100. Rough calc: tokens/sec ~ (1,200 * (180 tokens) / 10s session?) — okay this is getting messy. But practically, we translate to GPU-seconds required per minute. For POC we'll run the bench harness on a representative sample to get empirical GPU throughput. Our rule of thumb: for streaming chat on a 13B-ish model you might see 8-12 concurrent sessions per GPU at acceptable latency.
05:28 Maya: So for our expected peak, what would that mean?
05:31 Evan: If you have 1,200 concurrent, at 10 sessions/GPU you'd need ~120 GPUs, which is obviously large. But most deployments use session multiplexing, and actual concurrency is lower because not all sessions are actively generating tokens simultaneously. With batching and KV cache we often see effective concurrency increase 2x. So the POC is critical to get the actual numbers.
05:55 Rafael: That number 120 seems unrealistic for POC — what are typical POCs we do with mid-market customers?
06:01 Samira: Usually 2-8 GPUs reserved with burst to 16-32 for spikes. For Acme we might start with a higher baseline if your traces justify it; otherwise we simulate via synthetic load to validate autoscaler.
06:15 Priya: Could we do hybrid: reserved baseline 4 GPUs for predictable throughput, burst up to 24 GPUs for spikes, and fallback to quantized models if queue length exceeds threshold?
06:26 Jordan: That sounds like a good POC config. We'll test with both the nominal model and the quantized fallback. We'll also add a warm pool of 1 GPU to accelerate burst starts.
06:40 Tom: How do you trigger fallback automatically? Is it queue length, latency, or cost threshold?
06:46 Samira: We support policy-based routing: thresholds on queue length, tail latency, or cost per token. E.g., fallback if p95 > 350ms for >30s, or if queue length > N. Policies are configurable per-route.
07:05 Rafael: Any concerns about model state consistency when falling back? We use session-level context a lot.
07:12 Evan: Good point. We ensure prefix cache and serialized KV format compatibility across model variants when possible; older architectures may not support identical KV semantics so we treat those as best-effort and include evaluation for regressions.
07:30 Priya: For quantization, do you have recommended quant profiles? int8-lower-bit? We care about hallucination increase.
07:37 Samira: We have recommended profiles per model; for many Llama-family models int8 is reasonable with small quality delta, but we always evaluate on your labeled prompts. We'll put suggested profiles in the benchmark doc.
07:50 Maya: On instrumentation — can we get token-level cost and latency per request, and per-route dashboards?
07:56 Jordan: Yes that's part of the console: token breakdown, per-request latency heatmaps, and model-level cost. We'll share demo screenshots.
08:05 Rafael: Regarding benchmarks, what exact workloads do you recommend?
08:09 Samira: Three workloads: 1) Steady traffic at your typical qps for 30-60m to measure steady-state efficiency. 2) Spike profile: synthetic 5-10x bursts for short durations to validate burst+fallback. 3) Quality eval: run labeled prompt set across model variants to track correctness/hallucination.
08:30 Priya: We'll prepare the labeled set for the quality eval.
08:33 Jordan: Great. We'll also provide a sample Jupyter that runs the bench harness against a small canary cluster.
08:42 Maya: How much engineer time will you need from our side during the POC?
08:47 Jordan: Typical: 3-5 hours/week from infra + 2-4 hours/week from ML owner for evals. First two weeks require more to set up tracing and provide traces.
09:00 Rafael: About rollback and safety — if we find regressions during fallback, what's the plan?
09:04 Samira: We'll keep canary traffic split; automatic rollback policy exists — if quality metric drops below threshold we'll revert to previous model and alert. Also we keep full audit logs so you can trace prompts.
09:18 Tom: One more infra question: do you support warm standby in region B for failover?
09:22 Jordan: Yes, multi-region standby is supported for Dedicated/Private deployments. We can plan a warm standby but cost goes up. For POC we usually test single-region resilience.
09:32 Priya: Ok recapping success criteria: p95 < 350ms during clinician window, hallucination rate < X% on labeled set (we'll define), cost per session < $Y (TBD), availability 99.9% during window.
09:51 Jordan: I'll capture that and draft a success criteria doc.
09:55 Maya: Anything else on autoscaling tuning?
09:58 Evan: We'll tune autoscaler thresholds and batching windows; sometimes increasing batching window by 50-100ms gives big cost wins but trade latency for token throughput. We'll show the delta in the bench report.
10:14 Rafael: On pricing, can you outline reserved vs burst cost in a simple table?
10:18 Jordan: Yes, I'll send a worksheet with reserved hourly-equivalent and burst per-minute rates plus an example TCO calc using your traced traffic.
10:27 Priya: Do you have references for similar healthcare customers?
10:30 Jordan: We have a handful anonymized case studies — we'll include redacted notes and an architecture slide.
10:36 Maya: Sounds good. Next steps again?
10:38 Jordan: Action items — Jordan send pricing & reserved GPU worksheet; Samira share benchmark config and sample Jupyter; Rafael provide 7-day anonymized trace; schedule engineering workshop week of 3/24.
10:52 Maya: We'll aim to provide trace and internal stakeholders list by Monday. Thanks all.
11:00 Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and docs.
